history.heading: Peoples and the slave coast
paragraphs: Togo, a narrow country in West Africa between Ghana and Benin, was settled by peoples including the Ewe, who migrated from present-day Nigeria, and the Kabye in the north. The coast was part of the "Slave Coast" from which many Africans were shipped to the Americas. The Koutammakou landscape, with the distinctive mud tower-houses of the Batammariba, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.heading: German and French rule
paragraphs: Germany established the protectorate of Togoland in 1884 and developed it as a "model colony" with railways and plantations. After the First World War, it was divided between Britain (whose part later joined Ghana) and France.
French Togo became independent on 27 April 1960 under Sylvanus Olympio, who was assassinated in 1963 in one of Africa's first post-independence coups.

history.heading: The Gnassingbé era
paragraphs: Gnassingbé Eyadéma, who took part in the 1963 coup, seized power in 1967 and ruled until his death in 2005, one of Africa's longest-serving rulers. His son Faure Gnassingbé took over amid deadly protests and has ruled since. Constitutional changes in 2024 created a parliamentary system in which he became President of the Council of Ministers in 2025, with no term limits.

culture.heading: Traditions
paragraphs: Togo has around 40 ethnic groups. French is official, and Ewe and Kabye are national languages. Christianity, Islam and traditional religions, including Vodun, are practised. The Akodessewa fetish market in Lomé sells items used in traditional medicine. Fufu with sauces and grilled fish are common foods.

politics.heading: Dominant ruling family
paragraphs: Under the 2024 constitution, Togo is formally a parliamentary republic, with the President of the Council of Ministers holding executive power, chosen by parliament, which is dominated by the ruling party. The opposition calls the change a way for Faure Gnassingbé to stay in power indefinitely; protests in 2025 were repressed.

economy.heading: Port and phosphates
paragraphs: The deep-water Port of Lomé is a major regional hub for West Africa. Phosphates, cotton, cocoa and coffee are key exports, and most people work in agriculture. Lomé has also become a financial centre, hosting headquarters of pan-African banks. The currency is the West African CFA franc.
